name: Hirudoid

lead:
Hirudoid is a brand of cream whose active ingredient is mucopolysaccharide polysulfate, a heparinoid. It is applied to the skin for bruises and superficial vein conditions, and appears in forum discussions of bruising after cosmetic procedures and injections. People use it to help bruises fade so the skin looks clear sooner.
Reviews describe topical heparinoids as acting on microcirculation, anti-inflammatory and antithrombotic pathways. A 2021 meta-analysis of 20 trials looked at the cream for non-exudative eczema, and a 1990 randomized trial compared Hirudoid with placebo and piroxicam gel in superficial thrombophlebitis.

paras: Applied as a cream to the affected skin as the product label directs. People discuss using it on bruises after procedures.
Topical use can cause local skin reactions. Product labels give guidance for broken skin and use with anticoagulants; check the label or a pharmacist.

chain: Heparinoid cream applied to bruised skin
angle.text: People apply Hirudoid to bruises hoping to clear discolouration faster, for example after procedures. Reviews describe circulation and anti-inflammatory effects of topical heparinoids.

lead: Hirudoid is a heparinoid cream built on mucopolysaccharide polysulfate (MPS), used for bruises, superficial thrombophlebitis and venous disorders.[1][2] People use it for the appearance benefit of faster-clearing bruises.

A 2025 review says topical heparin and heparinoid products provide anticoagulation, improve microcirculation and regulate skin permeability, and that MPS offers similar vascular benefits with antithrombotic and anti-inflammatory actions.[1] An earlier review found heparin gel 1000 IU/g more effective than placebo in superficial thrombophlebitis and superior to the heparinoid cream Hirudoid in one head-to-head comparison.[2]

In a meta-analysis of 20 randomized trials, MPS cream gave a higher efficacy rate, lower recurrence and lower itch score than urea cream or vaseline for non-exudative eczema.[3] A mouse study reported that a heparinoid-containing product improved epidermal barrier recovery.[4]

paras: Medical uses include superficial thrombophlebitis and venous disorders,[1][2][5] and as a moisturiser in eczema.[3]
Topical heparinoids are described as anticoagulant, microcirculation-enhancing and anti-inflammatory, with effects influenced by concentration and formulation.[1]

A 1990 comparative trial tested placebo, Hirudoid cream and piroxicam gel in superficial thrombophlebitis.[5] A 2021 meta-analysis of 20 RCTs covers MPS cream in non-exudative eczema.[3] A 2008 review pooled 20 studies of topical heparins in 1055 patients.[2] No trials have examined bruise appearance directly.
